name: Central opercular cortex
summary: The central operculum is the part of the precentral and postcentral gyri that folds under to form the roof of the middle portion of the lateral sulcus, immediately above the insula. It contains the ventral end of the primary motor and sensory maps, the face, tongue, larynx and pharynx representations, and the secondary somatosensory cortex lies just behind it in the parietal operculum. Lesions produce contralateral lower facial weakness, dysarthria and dysphagia and loss of sensation on the face, and bilateral lesions cause the anarthric opercular syndrome; middle cerebral artery branch infarcts and perisylvian polymicrogyria are the common causes.

anatomy.location: The buried inferior ends of the precentral and postcentral gyri above the insula, between the frontal operculum in front and the parietal operculum behind, forming the upper bank of the posterior Sylvian fissure.

efferents.to: Facial, hypoglossal, ambiguus and trigeminal motor nuclei

function: The lower end of the motor homunculus here drives the muscles of the face, jaw, tongue, larynx and pharynx through the corticobulbar tract, mostly bilaterally except for the lower face, and the adjacent sensory strip receives touch and proprioception from the face and mouth through the ventral posteromedial thalamus. The region controls the fine sequencing of speech and swallowing, and its secondary somatosensory field integrates pain and touch from both sides of the body. Focal seizures here produce contralateral facial clonic jerking, tongue tingling and drooling that may march to the arm.

bestView.label: central operculum above the posterior insula
buried ends of the central gyri at the Sylvian fissure

imaging.normalAppearance: The lower ends of the precentral and postcentral gyri as they curve into the Sylvian fissure, best seen on coronal images through the posterior insula; the face motor area is at the lateral convexity above the fissure.

pathology.pathology: MCA branch infarct with facial weakness and dysarthria
pathology.finding: Small cortical restricted diffusion at the inferior end of the central gyri; often mistaken clinically for a brainstem or peripheral facial lesion.
Thickened irregular cortex with shallow sulci around the Sylvian fissures, often bilateral, with pseudobulbar palsy and epilepsy from childhood.

pathology.pathology: Focal motor seizure of the face
pathology.finding: Clonic jerking of the contralateral face with drooling and speech arrest; EEG shows a fronto-central focus.

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral lower facial weakness sparing the forehead
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the crossed corticobulbar projection to the lower facial motor nucleus
Weakness and incoordination of the tongue, palate and pharynx from the ventral motor cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of touch and position sense on the face and in the mouth
lesionEffects.mechanism: Damage to the ventral postcentral gyrus receiving the VPM thalamic projection

examination: Test the lower face: show the teeth, puff the cheeks; forehead sparing points to a supranuclear lesion
Palatal movement, gag, swallowing and tongue power and speed
Facial two-point discrimination and stereognosis of objects in the mouth
pearls: A central facial palsy with dysarthria and a normal arm can be a tiny opercular cortical stroke
Bilateral opercular damage causes pseudobulbar palsy of cortical origin with intact emotional facial movement
The face area lies low on the convexity, just above the Sylvian fissure, in the inferior division of the MCA

pitfalls: Forehead sparing distinguishes a cortical facial palsy from a Bell palsy, but a partial peripheral palsy can mimic it; check taste and hyperacusis
